Dynamic Optimal Transport

Optimal transport becomes especially powerful once distances between measures are seen as actions of moving mass. This chapter first develops the dynamic language: continuity equations describe admissible measure evolutions, while the Benamou--Brenier formula identifies W2\Wass_2W2​ with a least-action principle. These ideas prepare the gradient-flow and generative-model chapters that follow.

Guiding Comparison

The static formulation optimizes over a coupling between endpoints. The dynamic formulation optimizes over a whole path of measures and a velocity field. The continuity equation is the constraint, and kinetic energy is the cost.

Evolutions Over the Space of Measures¶

We start with the continuity equation because it is the common language for particles, densities and weak measure evolutions. It also makes precise which velocity fields actually move mass.

Lagrangian and Eulerian Descriptions¶

Consider an evolution t↦αt∈P(Rd)t\mapsto\alpha_t\in\mathcal P(\RR^d)t↦αt​∈P(Rd). It can be described in a Lagrangian way as the advection of particles along a time-dependent vector field vt(x)v_t(x)vt​(x):

 dx(t) dt=vt(x(t)).\frac{\d x(t)}{\d t}=v_t(x(t)).dtdx(t)​=vt​(x(t)).
(1)

Writing TtT_tTt​ for the associated flow map, so that Tt(x(0))=x(t)T_t(x(0))=x(t)Tt​(x(0))=x(t), the advected measure is

αt=(Tt)♯α0.\alpha_t=(T_t)_\sharp\alpha_0.αt​=(Tt​)♯​α0​.
(2)

For empirical measures, αt=n−1∑i=1nδxi(t)\alpha_t=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i(t)}αt​=n−1∑i=1n​δxi​(t)​, each particle solves (1).

In the Eulerian description, the same motion is written directly on the evolving measure:

∂αt∂t+div⁡(vtαt)=0.\frac{\partial\alpha_t}{\partial t} +\operatorname{div}(v_t\alpha_t)=0.∂t∂αt​​+div(vt​αt​)=0.
(3)

This PDE is often called the advection equation, the continuity equation, or Liouville’s equation when it acts on phase space. It is a classical PDE only when αt\alpha_tαt​ has a smooth density. For general measures, and in particular for empirical measures, it is understood weakly: for any smooth test function (t,x)↦φ(t,x)(t,x)\mapsto\varphi(t,x)(t,x)↦φ(t,x) compactly supported in time,

∫01 ⁣∫Rd(∂tφ(t,x)+⟨vt(x),∇xφ(t,x)⟩) dαt(x) dt=0.\int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d} \left( \partial_t\varphi(t,x) +\dotp{v_t(x)}{\nabla_x\varphi(t,x)} \right) \d\alpha_t(x)\d t =0.∫01​∫Rd​(∂t​φ(t,x)+⟨vt​(x),∇x​φ(t,x)⟩)dαt​(x)dt=0.
(4)

This weak equation is obtained from (3) by integration by parts. For smooth positive densities, the classical and weak formulations are equivalent; for particle clouds, the weak form remains meaningful.

Proposition: Lagrangian Flows Solve the Continuity Equation

Consider a smooth flow Tt:Rd→RdT_t:\RR^d\to\RR^dTt​:Rd→Rd and define αt=(Tt)♯α0\alpha_t=(T_t)_\sharp\alpha_0αt​=(Tt​)♯​α0​. Define the Eulerian velocity field by

vt(Tt(y))=∂tTt(y).v_t(T_t(y))=\partial_t T_t(y).vt​(Tt​(y))=∂t​Tt​(y).
(5)

Then (αt,vt)(\alpha_t,v_t)(αt​,vt​) solves the continuity equation in the weak sense (4). In particular, if α0=n−1∑iδxi(0)\alpha_0=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(0)}α0​=n−1∑i​δxi​(0)​ is empirical, then αt=n−1∑iδxi(t)\alpha_t=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i(t)}αt​=n−1∑i​δxi​(t)​ is empirical as well, with particle velocities x˙i(t)=vt(xi(t))\dot x_i(t)=v_t(x_i(t))x˙i​(t)=vt​(xi​(t)).

Proof

Let φ(t,x)\varphi(t,x)φ(t,x) be a smooth test function vanishing at t=0t=0t=0 and t=1t=1t=1. Since αt=(Tt)♯α0\alpha_t=(T_t)_\sharp\alpha_0αt​=(Tt​)♯​α0​,

 d dt∫φ(t,x) dαt(x)= d dt∫φ(t,Tt(y)) dα0(y).\frac{\d}{\d t}\int \varphi(t,x)\d\alpha_t(x) = \frac{\d}{\d t}\int \varphi(t,T_t(y))\d\alpha_0(y).dtd​∫φ(t,x)dαt​(x)=dtd​∫φ(t,Tt​(y))dα0​(y).

 d dt∫φ(t,Tt(y)) dα0(y)=∫(∂tφ(t,Tt(y))+⟨∇xφ(t,Tt(y)),∂tTt(y)⟩) dα0(y).\frac{\d}{\d t}\int \varphi(t,T_t(y))\d\alpha_0(y) = \int \left( \partial_t\varphi(t,T_t(y)) +\dotp{\nabla_x\varphi(t,T_t(y))}{\partial_t T_t(y)} \right) \d\alpha_0(y).dtd​∫φ(t,Tt​(y))dα0​(y)=∫(∂t​φ(t,Tt​(y))+⟨∇x​φ(t,Tt​(y)),∂t​Tt​(y)⟩)dα0​(y).

From Measure Evolutions to Vector Fields¶

For a given evolution (αt)t(\alpha_t)_t(αt​)t​, there are typically infinitely many velocity fields vtv_tvt​ satisfying

∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0.\partial_t\alpha_t+\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)=0.∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0.
(9)

This non-uniqueness comes from the kernel of the weighted divergence. The linear space of vector fields that leave a measure α\alphaα invariant is

Hα={v:div⁡(αv)=0}.\mathcal H_\alpha = \{v:\operatorname{div}(\alpha v)=0\}.Hα​={v:div(αv)=0}.
(10)

It is usually non-trivial: if α\alphaα is an isotropic Gaussian, Hα\mathcal H_\alphaHα​ contains rotational vector fields generated by anti-symmetric matrices.

Dacorogna--Moser Inversion¶

Reconstructing particles from an observed density evolution is therefore ill-posed. A simple choice, introduced by Dacorogna and Moser Dacorogna & Moser, 1990, imposes that the flux αtvt\alpha_t v_tαt​vt​ is a gradient field. Formally,

vt=−1αt∇Δ−1(∂tαt),v_t = -\frac{1}{\alpha_t} \nabla\Delta^{-1}(\partial_t\alpha_t),vt​=−αt​1​∇Δ−1(∂t​αt​),
(11)

with suitable boundary conditions, for instance vanishing at infinity. This formula is useful conceptually but delicate when αt\alpha_tαt​ vanishes, and it does not generally produce a gradient velocity field.

The classical Dacorogna--Moser construction uses the linear density path. If αi=ρi  dx\alpha_i=\rho_i\,\d xαi​=ρi​dx are smooth positive densities with the same total mass on a bounded domain Ω\OmegaΩ, set

αt=(1−t)α0+tα1=ρt  dx,ρt=(1−t)ρ0+tρ1.\alpha_t=(1-t)\alpha_0+t\alpha_1=\rho_t\,\d x, \qquad \rho_t=(1-t)\rho_0+t\rho_1.αt​=(1−t)α0​+tα1​=ρt​dx,ρt​=(1−t)ρ0​+tρ1​.
(12)

Choose a time-independent flux www satisfying

div⁡w=ρ0−ρ1,w⋅n=0on ∂Ω,\operatorname{div} w=\rho_0-\rho_1, \qquad w\cdot n=0\quad\hbox{on }\partial\Omega,divw=ρ0​−ρ1​,w⋅n=0on ∂Ω,
(13)

for instance w=−∇ϕw=-\nabla\phiw=−∇ϕ with Δϕ=ρ1−ρ0\Delta\phi=\rho_1-\rho_0Δϕ=ρ1​−ρ0​ and Neumann boundary condition. Then

vt=wρtv_t=\frac{w}{\rho_t}vt​=ρt​w​
(14)

satisfies ∂tρt+div⁡(ρtvt)=0\partial_t\rho_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho_t v_t)=0∂t​ρt​+div(ρt​vt​)=0. The flow ∂tTt=vt∘Tt\partial_t T_t=v_t\circ T_t∂t​Tt​=vt​∘Tt​, T0=Id⁡T_0=\operatorname{Id}T0​=Id, therefore transports ρ0 dx\rho_0\d xρ0​dx onto ρt dx\rho_t\d xρt​dx, and T1T_1T1​ solves the prescribed-Jacobian problem ρ1(T1(x))det⁡(∇T1(x))=ρ0(x)\rho_1(T_1(x))\det(\nabla T_1(x))=\rho_0(x)ρ1​(T1​(x))det(∇T1​(x))=ρ0​(x).

Least-Square Inversion and Gradient Structure¶

A more robust choice, used implicitly in flow matching, optimal transport and Wasserstein gradient flows, is to select among all admissible velocities the one with smallest kinetic energy:

min⁡v12∫01 ⁣∫Rd∥vt(x)∥2  dαt(x) dtsubject to∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0.\min_v \frac12\int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d}\norm{v_t(x)}^2\,\d\alpha_t(x)\d t \quad \text{subject to} \quad \partial_t\alpha_t+\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)=0.vmin​21​∫01​∫Rd​∥vt​(x)∥2dαt​(x)dtsubject to∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0.
(15)
Proposition: Least-Square Velocities Are Gradients

Assume that αt=ρt  dx\alpha_t=\rho_t\,\d xαt​=ρt​dx is a smooth positive density curve and that boundary terms vanish. The minimizer of (15), if it exists, is a gradient field

vt=∇ϕt,v_t=\nabla\phi_t,vt​=∇ϕt​,
(16)

where ϕt\phi_tϕt​, unique up to an additive constant, solves the weighted Poisson equation

−div⁡(ρt∇ϕt)=∂tρt,vt=−∇Δαt−1(∂tαt),Δαtϕ=div⁡(αt∇ϕ).-\operatorname{div}(\rho_t\nabla\phi_t)=\partial_t\rho_t, \qquad v_t=-\nabla\Delta_{\alpha_t}^{-1}(\partial_t\alpha_t), \qquad \Delta_{\alpha_t}\phi=\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t\nabla\phi).−div(ρt​∇ϕt​)=∂t​ρt​,vt​=−∇Δαt​−1​(∂t​αt​),Δαt​​ϕ=div(αt​∇ϕ).
(17)
Proof

Introduce a Lagrange multiplier ϕt\phi_tϕt​ for the continuity equation. The constrained problem has the formal saddle formulation

min⁡vmax⁡ϕ∫01[12∫Rd∥vt(x)∥2  dαt(x)+∫Rdϕt(x)(div⁡(αtvt)(x)+∂tαt(x)) dx] dt.\min_v\max_\phi \int_0^1 \left[ \frac12\int_{\RR^d}\norm{v_t(x)}^2\,\d\alpha_t(x) + \int_{\RR^d}\phi_t(x) \left(\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)(x)+\partial_t\alpha_t(x)\right) \d x \right]\d t.vmin​ϕmax​∫01​[21​∫Rd​∥vt​(x)∥2dαt​(x)+∫Rd​ϕt​(x)(div(αt​vt​)(x)+∂t​αt​(x))dx]dt.
(18)

Integrating by parts in the divergence term gives, for each ttt,

∫(12∥vt∥2−⟨∇ϕt,vt⟩) dαt+∫ϕt ∂tαt.\int \left( \frac12\norm{v_t}^2-\dotp{\nabla\phi_t}{v_t} \right) \d\alpha_t + \int\phi_t\,\partial_t\alpha_t.∫(21​∥vt​∥2−⟨∇ϕt​,vt​⟩)dαt​+∫ϕt​∂t​αt​.
(19)

The pointwise minimizer in vtv_tvt​ is therefore vt=∇ϕtv_t=\nabla\phi_tvt​=∇ϕt​. Substituting this into ∂tρt+div⁡(ρtvt)=0\partial_t\rho_t+\operatorname{div}(\rho_t v_t)=0∂t​ρt​+div(ρt​vt​)=0 gives the weighted Poisson equation in (17). The inverse notation is a shorthand for solving this equation on zero-mean right-hand sides, modulo additive constants.

In general this inversion is still computationally demanding, but special choices of (αt)t(\alpha_t)_t(αt​)t​ lead to simpler formulas; this is the mechanism exploited later by flow matching in Section Generative Models via Flow Matching.

Algorithm: Least-square velocity reconstruction

Input: Smooth positive density curve (ρt)t∈[0,1](\rho_t)_{t\in[0,1]}(ρt​)t∈[0,1]​ and boundary conditions.

Output: Minimal-energy velocity field vtv_tvt​ realizing the curve.

For each time ttt do:

Compute ∂tρt\partial_t\rho_t∂t​ρt​.

Solve weighted Poisson equation:

−div⁡(ρt∇ϕt)=∂tρt,∫ϕtρt=0.-\diverg(\rho_t\nabla\phi_t)=\partial_t\rho_t, \qquad \int\phi_t\rho_t=0.−div(ρt​∇ϕt​)=∂t​ρt​,∫ϕt​ρt​=0.

Set vt=∇ϕt.v_t=\nabla\phi_t .vt​=∇ϕt​.

Return (vt)t∈[0,1](v_t)_{t\in[0,1]}(vt​)t∈[0,1]​.

Benamou--Brenier Dynamic Formulation of OT¶

The dynamic formulation identifies W2\Wass_2W2​ with the kinetic energy of the cheapest continuity-equation path. It is the point where OT becomes a least-action principle.

Benamou--Brenier Formulation¶

Instead of assuming that a whole curve (αt)t∈[0,1](\alpha_t)_{t\in[0,1]}(αt​)t∈[0,1]​ is prescribed, one fixes only the endpoints α0\alpha_0α0​ and α1\alpha_1α1​ and minimizes the least-square energy (15). The theorem of Benamou and Brenier states that this geodesic energy is exactly the squared Wasserstein distance Benamou & Brenier, 2000.

Theorem: Benamou--Brenier

For probability measures α0,α1∈P2(Rd)\alpha_0,\alpha_1\in\mathcal P_2(\RR^d)α0​,α1​∈P2​(Rd),

W22(α0,α1)=inf⁡(αt,vt)∫01 ⁣∫Rd∥vt(x)∥2  dαt(x) dt,\Wass_2^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{(\alpha_t,v_t)} \int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d}\norm{v_t(x)}^2\,\d\alpha_t(x)\d t,W22​(α0​,α1​)=(αt​,vt​)inf​∫01​∫Rd​∥vt​(x)∥2dαt​(x)dt,
(20)

where the infimum is over (αt,vt)(\alpha_t,v_t)(αt​,vt​) solving ∂tαt+∇ ⁣⋅(αtvt)=0\partial_t\alpha_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\alpha_t v_t)=0∂t​αt​+∇⋅(αt​vt​)=0 with αt=0=α0\alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0αt=0​=α0​ and αt=1=α1\alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1αt=1​=α1​. If α0\alpha_0α0​ has a density and TTT is the optimal Monge map T♯α0=α1T_\sharp\alpha_0=\alpha_1T♯​α0​=α1​, the minimizer is

αt=((1−t)Id+tT)♯α0,vt((1−t)x+tT(x))=T(x)−x.\alpha_t=((1-t)\Id+tT)_\sharp\alpha_0, \qquad v_t((1-t)x+tT(x))=T(x)-x.αt​=((1−t)Id+tT)♯​α0​,vt​((1−t)x+tT(x))=T(x)−x.
(21)
Proof

For the inequality “dynamic ≤\leq≤ static”, assume first that a Monge map TTT exists and define (αt,vt)(\alpha_t,v_t)(αt​,vt​) by (21). Since the Lagrangian velocity T(x)−xT(x)-xT(x)−x is independent of ttt,

∫01 ⁣∫∥vt∥2  dαt dt=∫∥T(x)−x∥2  dα0(x),\int_0^1\!\int\norm{v_t}^2\,\d\alpha_t\d t = \int\norm{T(x)-x}^2\,\d\alpha_0(x),∫01​∫∥vt​∥2dαt​dt=∫∥T(x)−x∥2dα0​(x),
(22)

so the dynamic cost is no larger than the static Monge cost. Without a Monge map, the same construction uses an optimal coupling π\piπ: sample (X,Y)∼π(X,Y)\sim\pi(X,Y)∼π and move along the straight path γX,Y(t)=(1−t)X+tY\gamma_{X,Y}(t)=(1-t)X+tYγX,Y​(t)=(1−t)X+tY. This path measure has action ∫∥x−y∥2 dπ(x,y)\int\norm{x-y}^2\d\pi(x,y)∫∥x−y∥2dπ(x,y); projecting path velocities onto their conditional mean at time ttt gives an admissible Eulerian velocity with no larger action, so the dynamic value is no larger than the Kantorovich value.

Conversely, for a smooth deterministic path, take the flow TtT_tTt​ defined by T˙t=vt∘Tt\dot T_t=v_t\circ T_tT˙t​=vt​∘Tt​ and T0=IdT_0=\IdT0​=Id. Then αt=(Tt)♯α0\alpha_t=(T_t)_\sharp\alpha_0αt​=(Tt​)♯​α0​ and (T1)♯α0=α1(T_1)_\sharp\alpha_0=\alpha_1(T1​)♯​α0​=α1​. Jensen’s inequality gives

∥T1(x)−x∥2≤∫01∥vt(Tt(x))∥2 dt.\norm{T_1(x)-x}^2 \leq \int_0^1\norm{v_t(T_t(x))}^2\d t.∥T1​(x)−x∥2≤∫01​∥vt​(Tt​(x))∥2dt.
(23)

After integration with respect to α0\alpha_0α0​, the Monge cost is bounded above by the dynamic action. For general finite-energy solutions of the continuity equation, the superposition principle lifts the curve to a probability measure on absolutely continuous paths; applying Jensen’s inequality pathwise gives a coupling of the endpoints whose quadratic cost is no larger than the action. Thus the Kantorovich value is bounded above by the dynamic value.

Convex Moment-Based Reformulation¶

Although (20) is not jointly convex in (αt,vt)(\alpha_t,v_t)(αt​,vt​), it becomes convex after replacing velocities by the momentum measure mt=vtαtm_t=v_t\alpha_tmt​=vt​αt​ and using the perspective action. In the absolutely continuous case αt=ρt  dx\alpha_t=\rho_t\,\d xαt​=ρt​dx and mt(x)=ρt(x)vt(x)m_t(x)=\rho_t(x)v_t(x)mt​(x)=ρt​(x)vt​(x),

W22(α0,α1)=inf⁡∂tρt+div⁡mt=0ρt=0dx=α0, ρt=1dx=α1∫01 ⁣∫Rd∥mt(x)∥2ρt(x) dx  dt,\Wass_2^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\rho_t+\operatorname{div}m_t=0\\ \rho_{t=0}\d x=\alpha_0,\ \rho_{t=1}\d x=\alpha_1}} \int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d} \frac{\norm{m_t(x)}^2}{\rho_t(x)} \d x\,\d t,W22​(α0​,α1​)=∂t​ρt​+divmt​=0ρt=0​dx=α0​, ρt=1​dx=α1​​inf​∫01​∫Rd​ρt​(x)∥mt​(x)∥2​dxdt,
(24)

with the usual convention that the integrand is 0 when (ρt,mt)=(0,0)(\rho_t,m_t)=(0,0)(ρt​,mt​)=(0,0) and +∞+\infty+∞ when ρt=0\rho_t=0ρt​=0 but mt≠0m_t\neq0mt​=0. For singular endpoints or curves, the same statement is interpreted with vector-valued momentum measures and the corresponding recession convention. This convex reformulation enables geodesic interpolation by convex optimization once the domain is discretized.

Dual Hamilton--Jacobi Formulation¶

The momentum formulation also has a useful dual. It turns the least-action problem into a Hamilton--Jacobi subsolution inequality for a scalar potential, with equality on the part of space-time actually visited by the optimal curve. With the no-1/21/21/2 convention of (24), the constants are as follows.

Proposition: Dual Benamou--Brenier Problem

Assume, for simplicity, that the densities are smooth, compactly supported, and that boundary terms vanish. Then the convex dynamic value has the dual formulation

W22(α0,α1)=sup⁡ϕ{∫Rdϕ1  dα1−∫Rdϕ0  dα0  :  ∂tϕt+14∥∇ϕt∥2≤0}.\Wass_2^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \sup_{\phi} \left\{ \int_{\RR^d}\phi_1\,\d\alpha_1 - \int_{\RR^d}\phi_0\,\d\alpha_0 \;:\; \partial_t\phi_t+\frac14\norm{\nabla\phi_t}^2\leq 0 \right\}.W22​(α0​,α1​)=ϕsup​{∫Rd​ϕ1​dα1​−∫Rd​ϕ0​dα0​:∂t​ϕt​+41​∥∇ϕt​∥2≤0}.
(25)

If (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m) and ϕ\phiϕ are smooth primal and dual optimizers, then

mt=ρt2∇ϕt,∂tϕt+14∥∇ϕt∥2=0on {ρt>0}.m_t=\frac{\rho_t}{2}\nabla\phi_t, \qquad \partial_t\phi_t+\frac14\norm{\nabla\phi_t}^2=0 \quad\text{on }\{\rho_t>0\}.mt​=2ρt​​∇ϕt​,∂t​ϕt​+41​∥∇ϕt​∥2=0on {ρt​>0}.
(26)

Equivalently, the optimal Eulerian velocity is vt=mt/ρt=∇ϕt/2v_t=m_t/\rho_t=\nabla\phi_t/2vt​=mt​/ρt​=∇ϕt​/2.

Proof

Let (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m) satisfy the continuity equation and let ϕ\phiϕ be smooth. Multiplying the constraint by ϕ\phiϕ and integrating by parts gives

∫Rdϕ1  dα1−∫Rdϕ0  dα0=∫01 ⁣∫Rd(ρt ∂tϕt+⟨mt,∇ϕt⟩) dx dt.\int_{\RR^d}\phi_1\,\d\alpha_1 - \int_{\RR^d}\phi_0\,\d\alpha_0 = \int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d} \left(\rho_t\,\partial_t\phi_t+\dotp{m_t}{\nabla\phi_t}\right)\d x\d t .∫Rd​ϕ1​dα1​−∫Rd​ϕ0​dα0​=∫01​∫Rd​(ρt​∂t​ϕt​+⟨mt​,∇ϕt​⟩)dxdt.
(27)

If ∂tϕt+∥∇ϕt∥2/4≤0\partial_t\phi_t+\norm{\nabla\phi_t}^2/4\leq0∂t​ϕt​+∥∇ϕt​∥2/4≤0, Young’s inequality yields

ρ ∂tϕ+⟨m,∇ϕ⟩≤−ρ4∥∇ϕ∥2+⟨m,∇ϕ⟩≤∥m∥2ρ,\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\dotp{m}{\nabla\phi} \leq -\frac{\rho}{4}\norm{\nabla\phi}^2+\dotp{m}{\nabla\phi} \leq \frac{\norm m^2}{\rho},ρ∂t​ϕ+⟨m,∇ϕ⟩≤−4ρ​∥∇ϕ∥2+⟨m,∇ϕ⟩≤ρ∥m∥2​,
(28)

with the usual perspective convention. Thus the dual objective of every feasible potential is no larger than the action of every feasible primal pair. Conversely, introducing ϕ\phiϕ as a Lagrange multiplier for ∂tρ+div⁡m=0\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}m=0∂t​ρ+divm=0, and discarding the fixed endpoint contribution, the pointwise minimization contains ∥m∥2/ρ−ρ ∂tϕ−⟨m,∇ϕ⟩\norm m^2/\rho-\rho\,\partial_t\phi-\dotp{m}{\nabla\phi}∥m∥2/ρ−ρ∂t​ϕ−⟨m,∇ϕ⟩. Minimizing over mmm gives m=ρ∇ϕ/2m=\rho\nabla\phi/2m=ρ∇ϕ/2; minimizing over ρ≥0\rho\geq0ρ≥0 is finite exactly under ∂tϕ+∥∇ϕ∥2/4≤0\partial_t\phi+\norm{\nabla\phi}^2/4\leq0∂t​ϕ+∥∇ϕ∥2/4≤0. Fenchel--Rockafellar duality then gives no duality gap in finite-dimensional discretizations. The continuum identity follows by the usual relaxation and approximation, with ϕ\phiϕ interpreted as a Hamilton--Jacobi subsolution. Equality in the two pointwise inequalities gives (26).

The inequality in (25) is the subsolution form of the Hamilton--Jacobi equation associated with the Hamiltonian H(p)=∥p∥2/4H(p)=\norm{p}^2/4H(p)=∥p∥2/4. On the transported mass, equality holds and the characteristics satisfy x˙=∇pH(∇ϕ)=∇ϕ/2\dot x=\nabla_pH(\nabla\phi)=\nabla\phi/2x˙=∇p​H(∇ϕ)=∇ϕ/2. Since this Hamiltonian is independent of xxx in Euclidean space, the momentum along characteristics is constant and the trajectories are straight lines. On a Riemannian manifold, the same duality uses the Hamiltonian Hx(p)=∥p∥gx−12/4H_x(p)=\norm{p}_{g_x^{-1}}^2/4Hx​(p)=∥p∥gx−1​2​/4; the characteristics are then geodesics for the underlying metric.

This also recovers the static Kantorovich inequality from a dynamic principle. If γ\gammaγ is any smooth curve with γ(0)=x\gamma(0)=xγ(0)=x and γ(1)=y\gamma(1)=yγ(1)=y, then

 d dtϕt(γ(t))=∂tϕt(γ(t))+⟨∇ϕt(γ(t)),γ˙(t)⟩≤∥γ˙(t)∥2.\frac{\d}{\d t}\phi_t(\gamma(t)) = \partial_t\phi_t(\gamma(t))+\dotp{\nabla\phi_t(\gamma(t))}{\dot\gamma(t)} \leq \norm{\dot\gamma(t)}^2.dtd​ϕt​(γ(t))=∂t​ϕt​(γ(t))+⟨∇ϕt​(γ(t)),γ˙​(t)⟩≤∥γ˙​(t)∥2.
(29)

After integration and minimization over curves,

ϕ1(y)−ϕ0(x)≤∥x−y∥2.\phi_1(y)-\phi_0(x)\leq \norm{x-y}^2.ϕ1​(y)−ϕ0​(x)≤∥x−y∥2.
(30)

Thus (ϕ0,ϕ1)(\phi_0,\phi_1)(ϕ0​,ϕ1​) is a feasible static Kantorovich dual pair for the quadratic cost. At optimality the inequality is saturated on the endpoint pairs connected by the primal characteristics.

Proximal Splitting¶

The convex momentum formulation also explains the original Benamou--Brenier solver. After discretization, the ALG2 scheme can be read as a Douglas--Rachford splitting, equivalently ADMM on the Fenchel--Rockafellar dual Papadakis et al., 2014. Suppressing discretization indices, write U=(ρ,m)U=(\rho,m)U=(ρ,m), let F(U)\mathcal F(U)F(U) be the integral of the perspective action, and let G=ιC\mathcal G=\iota_{\mathcal C}G=ιC​ be the indicator of the affine continuity constraint with prescribed endpoints. The problem is min⁡UF(U)+G(U)\min_U \mathcal F(U)+\mathcal G(U)minU​F(U)+G(U).

The two proximal operators separate the nonlinear and linear parts: the prox of F\mathcal FF is local in (t,x)(t,x)(t,x) and amounts to the perspective proximal operator, whereas the prox of G\mathcal GG is the orthogonal projection onto the divergence equation and endpoint constraints. Douglas--Rachford alternates these two simple operations.

Algorithm: Douglas--Rachford for dynamic Benamou--Brenier

Input: Functionals F,G=ιC\mathcal F,\mathcal G=\iota_{\mathcal C}F,G=ιC​, proximal parameter τ>0\tau>0τ>0, initial field Z0Z^0Z0.

Output: Discrete density-momentum field U⋆U^\starU⋆.

For k=0,1,…k=0,1,\ldotsk=0,1,… do:

Uk+1=prox⁡τF(Zk).U^{k+1}=\prox_{\tau\mathcal F}(Z^k).Uk+1=proxτF​(Zk).

Project reflected point: U~k+1=prox⁡τG(2Uk+1−Zk)=Proj⁡C(2Uk+1−Zk).\widetilde U^{k+1} = \prox_{\tau\mathcal G}(2U^{k+1}-Z^k) = \Proj_{\mathcal C}(2U^{k+1}-Z^k).Uk+1=proxτG​(2Uk+1−Zk)=ProjC​(2Uk+1−Zk).

Update Zk+1=Zk+U~k+1−Uk+1.Z^{k+1}=Z^k+\widetilde U^{k+1}-U^{k+1}.Zk+1=Zk+Uk+1−Uk+1.

If ∥Uk+1−U~k+1∥≤tol\norm{U^{k+1}-\widetilde U^{k+1}}\leq\mathrm{tol}∥∥​Uk+1−Uk+1∥∥​≤tol then:

Return Uk+1U^{k+1}Uk+1.

Path-Space Formulation¶

Let S=C([0,1];Rd)\Ss=C([0,1];\RR^d)S=C([0,1];Rd) be the space of continuous paths endowed with the uniform topology. For t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]t∈[0,1] define the evaluation map

Pt:S→Rd,Pt(γ)=γ(t).P_t:\Ss\to\RR^d, \qquad P_t(\gamma)=\gamma(t).Pt​:S→Rd,Pt​(γ)=γ(t).
(31)

The Benamou--Brenier cost admits the equivalent formulation

W22(α0,α1)=inf⁡M∈P(S){∫S ⁣∫01∥γ˙(t)∥2 dt  dM(γ)  :  (P0)♯M=α0, (P1)♯M=α1}.\Wass_2^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{M\in\Pp(\Ss)} \enscond{ \int_{\Ss}\!\int_0^1\norm{\dot\gamma(t)}^2\d t\,\d M(\gamma) }{ (P_0)_\sharp M=\alpha_0,\ (P_1)_\sharp M=\alpha_1 }.W22​(α0​,α1​)=M∈P(S)inf​{∫S​∫01​∥γ˙​(t)∥2dtdM(γ):(P0​)♯​M=α0​, (P1​)♯​M=α1​}.
(32)

If α0\alpha_0α0​ has a density, the minimizer M∗M^*M∗ is unique. Its time marginals reproduce the optimal curve: αt=(Pt)♯M∗\alpha_t=(P_t)_\sharp M^*αt​=(Pt​)♯​M∗ for all ttt. Furthermore, for a.e. ttt, denoting Qt(γ)=γ˙(t)Q_t(\gamma)=\dot\gamma(t)Qt​(γ)=γ˙​(t) on absolutely continuous paths, the conditional law of the velocity is deterministic:

(Pt,Qt)♯M∗( dx, dq)=αt( dx)δvt∗(x)( dq),(P_t,Q_t)_\sharp M^*(\d x,\d q) = \alpha_t(\d x)\delta_{v_t^*(x)}(\d q),(Pt​,Qt​)♯​M∗(dx,dq)=αt​(dx)δvt∗​(x)​(dq),
(33)

where vt∗v_t^*vt∗​ is the optimal velocity field in the Benamou--Brenier formulation. Hence M∗M^*M∗ concentrates on straight-line geodesics and, for a.e. ttt, assigns exactly one direction at αt\alpha_tαt​-a.e. spatial point.

Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Distances¶

The quadratic Benamou--Brenier formula is only one instance of a broader dynamic language. By changing the local action, the mobility, the balance equation, the state graph or the allowed jumps, one obtains transport geometries adapted to constraints, reactions, Markov chains, normalized directions or nonlocal motion. The focus here is metric: we define the distances and record their basic properties. Their use as gradient-flow geometries is gathered later in Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Flows.

Local Tangent Actions¶

The common infinitesimal object behind these dynamic distances is a local action on tangent directions. Let TαT_\alphaTα​ denote the admissible tangent space at α\alphaα, for instance the L2(α)L^2(\alpha)L2(α)-closure of gradients for the usual W2\Wass_2W2​ geometry. Assume first that nearby measures are generated by maps (Id+tw)♯α(\Id+t w)_\sharp\alpha(Id+tw)♯​α, with w∈Tαw\in T_\alphaw∈Tα​, and that a distance or discrepancy ddd has the second-order tangent expansion

qα(w):=lim⁡t→0d2((Id+tw)♯α,α)t2,q_\alpha(w) \eqdef \lim_{t\to0} \frac{d^2\big((\Id+t w)_\sharp\alpha,\alpha\big)}{t^2},qα​(w):=t→0lim​t2d2((Id+tw)♯​α,α)​,
(34)

whenever this limit exists. The notation qαq_\alphaqα​ is broader than a quadratic form: it is the squared local norm, or more generally the squared local action, selected by ddd. For instance, for Wp\Wass_pWp​ with 1≤p<+∞1\leq p<+\infty1≤p<+∞, one has qα(w)=(∫∥w∥p dα)2/pq_\alpha(w)=(\int\norm{w}^p\d\alpha)^{2/p}qα​(w)=(∫∥w∥pdα)2/p; for the spectral distances studied below it is the square of the spectral tangent norm; and for local quadratic geometries it is represented by an operator QαQ_\alphaQα​.

The Riemannian, or Hilbertian, special case occurs when qαq_\alphaqα​ is quadratic. If its polarization is represented on TαT_\alphaTα​ by a positive self-adjoint operator Qα:Tα→TαQ_\alpha:T_\alpha\to T_\alphaQα​:Tα​→Tα​,

qα(w,z)=⟨Qαw,z⟩L2(α),q_\alpha(w,z) = \left\langle Q_\alpha w,z\right\rangle_{L^2(\alpha)},qα​(w,z)=⟨Qα​w,z⟩L2(α)​,
(35)

then the tangent expansion reads

d2((Id+tw)♯α,α)=t2⟨Qαw,w⟩L2(α)+o(t2).d^2\big((\Id+t w)_\sharp\alpha,\alpha\big) = t^2\left\langle Q_\alpha w,w\right\rangle_{L^2(\alpha)} +o(t^2).d2((Id+tw)♯​α,α)=t2⟨Qα​w,w⟩L2(α)​+o(t2).
(36)

This is the metric counterpart of a Riemannian tensor on the space of measures. Section Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Flows uses the same qαq_\alphaqα​ to define steepest-descent directions and the corresponding gradient-flow PDEs.

Geodesic Distances from Quadratic Tangent Norms¶

The quadratic case of the local action can be integrated along curves to define a geodesic distance. Keeping the continuity equation but replacing the usual infinitesimal norm ∫∥v∥2 dα\int\norm{v}^2\d\alpha∫∥v∥2dα by ⟨Qαv,v⟩L2(α)\langle Q_\alpha v,v\rangle_{L^2(\alpha)}⟨Qα​v,v⟩L2(α)​ leads to the formal geodesic value

DQ2(α0,α1):=inf⁡∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0αt=0=α0, αt=1=α1∫01⟨Qαtvt,vt⟩L2(αt) dt.\mathsf D_Q^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) \eqdef \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\alpha_t+\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)=0\\ \alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0,\ \alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1}} \int_0^1 \left\langle Q_{\alpha_t}v_t,v_t\right\rangle_{L^2(\alpha_t)} \d t .DQ2​(α0​,α1​):=∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0αt=0​=α0​, αt=1​=α1​​inf​∫01​⟨Qαt​​vt​,vt​⟩L2(αt​)​dt.
(37)

The usual W2\Wass_2W2​ geometry corresponds to TαT_\alphaTα​ being the Wasserstein tangent space and Qα=IdQ_\alpha=\IdQα​=Id. This viewpoint is useful later for gradient flows: changing QαQ_\alphaQα​ changes the meaning of steepest descent, as made explicit in (196). When α=ρ dx\alpha=\rho\d xα=ρdx, m=ρvm=\rho vm=ρv, and QαQ_\alphaQα​ acts by pointwise multiplication with a symmetric positive matrix field Bρ(x)B_\rho(x)Bρ​(x), the integrand becomes

⟨Qαv,v⟩L2(α)=∫m(x)⊤Bρ(x)m(x)ρ(x)  dx.\left\langle Q_\alpha v,v\right\rangle_{L^2(\alpha)} = \int \frac{m(x)^\top B_\rho(x)m(x)}{\rho(x)}\,\d x .⟨Qα​v,v⟩L2(α)​=∫ρ(x)m(x)⊤Bρ​(x)m(x)​dx.
(38)

Thus local quadratic Riemannian metrics are a special case of the convex action-density formalism below, with

AQ(ρ,m,x)=m⊤Bρ(x)mρ.A_Q(\rho,m,x)=\frac{m^\top B_\rho(x)m}{\rho}.AQ​(ρ,m,x)=ρm⊤Bρ​(x)m​.
(39)

For Bρ=IdB_\rho=\IdBρ​=Id, this reduces to the Benamou--Brenier density ∣m∣2/ρ|m|^2/\rho∣m∣2/ρ. The next paragraph uses the (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m) variables as the primitive objects. This is less geometric but more robust analytically: convexity and lower-semicontinuous relaxation become transparent, and nonquadratic, hence non-Riemannian, Finsler-type actions are included as well.

General Mobilities and Convex Action Densities¶

The local action formalism keeps the continuity equation but replaces the quadratic cost ∣m∣2/ρ|m|^2/\rho∣m∣2/ρ by a convex function of density and momentum. It contains the quadratic QαQ_\alphaQα​-construction above whenever QαQ_\alphaQα​ is a local multiplication operator, and it also covers infinitesimal lengths that are not induced by a Hilbert norm. Let I⊂[0,+∞)I\subset[0,+\infty)I⊂[0,+∞) be a convex interval of admissible densities and let

A:I×Rd→[0,+∞]A:I\times\RR^d\to[0,+\infty]A:I×Rd→[0,+∞]
(40)

be an extended-valued lower-semicontinuous convex function of (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m), even in the momentum variable, with A(ρ,0)=0A(\rho,0)=0A(ρ,0)=0. For smooth densities ρ0,ρ1\rho_0,\rho_1ρ0​,ρ1​ with the same total mass, define

AA(ρ0,ρ1):=inf⁡∂tρt+∇⋅mt=0ρt=0=ρ0, ρt=1=ρ1∫01 ⁣∫A(ρt(x),mt(x))  dx  dt.\mathcal A_A(\rho_0,\rho_1) \eqdef \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot m_t=0\\ \rho_{t=0}=\rho_0,\ \rho_{t=1}=\rho_1}} \int_0^1\!\int A(\rho_t(x),m_t(x))\,\d x\,\d t.AA​(ρ0​,ρ1​):=∂t​ρt​+∇⋅mt​=0ρt=0​=ρ0​, ρt=1​=ρ1​​inf​∫01​∫A(ρt​(x),mt​(x))dxdt.
(41)

The function AAA specifies how expensive it is to carry a momentum mmm through a local density ρ\rhoρ; values +∞+\infty+∞ encode forbidden states, such as moving mass through vacuum. Convexity is the structural assumption behind existence and stability of minimizers, and the same formula extends to measure-valued curves by lower-semicontinuous relaxation. The next proposition isolates when this action is a genuine path metric rather than only a variational principle.

For a smooth state α=ρ dx\alpha=\rho\d xα=ρdx and a velocity vvv, the associated instantaneous action is

ℓA,α(v):=∫A(ρ(x),ρ(x)v(x))  dx.\ell_{A,\alpha}(v) \eqdef \int A(\rho(x),\rho(x)v(x))\,\d x .ℓA,α​(v):=∫A(ρ(x),ρ(x)v(x))dx.
(42)

If AAA is rrr-homogeneous in the momentum and the distance is DA=AA1/r\mathsf D_A=\mathcal A_A^{1/r}DA​=AA1/r​, then the squared tangent cost in the notation of (34) is ℓA,α(v)2/r\ell_{A,\alpha}(v)^{2/r}ℓA,α​(v)2/r. Thus ℓA,α\ell_{A,\alpha}ℓA,α​ and qαq_\alphaqα​ coincide in the quadratic case r=2r=2r=2, but not for a general Wp\Wass_pWp​-type Finsler action. This convention keeps the metric definition here aligned with the steepest-descent notation used later in Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Flows.

Proposition: Homogeneous Dynamic Actions Define Distances

Assume, in addition to the hypotheses above, that for some q>1q>1q>1

A(ρ,λm)=∣λ∣qA(ρ,m)for all λ∈R,A(\rho,\lambda m)=|\lambda|^qA(\rho,m) \qquad \text{for all }\lambda\in\RR,A(ρ,λm)=∣λ∣qA(ρ,m)for all λ∈R,
(43)

and that A(ρ,m)=0A(\rho,m)=0A(ρ,m)=0 if and only if m=0m=0m=0. Set

DA(ρ0,ρ1):=AA(ρ0,ρ1)1/q.\mathsf D_A(\rho_0,\rho_1) \eqdef \mathcal A_A(\rho_0,\rho_1)^{1/q}.DA​(ρ0​,ρ1​):=AA​(ρ0​,ρ1​)1/q.
(44)

On every fixed-mass class, and after the usual lower-semicontinuous relaxation assuming that zero-action values are attained, DA\mathsf D_ADA​ is an extended distance on each finite-action component: it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and DA(ρ0,ρ1)=0\mathsf D_A(\rho_0,\rho_1)=0DA​(ρ0​,ρ1​)=0 only when ρ0=ρ1\rho_0=\rho_1ρ0​=ρ1​.

Proof

The constant curve gives zero self-distance. Conversely, zero relaxed action forces A(ρt,mt)=0A(\rho_t,m_t)=0A(ρt​,mt​)=0 a.e., hence mt=0m_t=0mt​=0 a.e.; the continuity equation then gives ∂tρt=0\partial_t\rho_t=0∂t​ρt​=0 and ρ0=ρ1\rho_0=\rho_1ρ0​=ρ1​. Symmetry follows by time reversal and the evenness of AAA in mmm. For the triangle inequality, concatenate an almost optimal curve from ρ0\rho_0ρ0​ to ρ1\rho_1ρ1​ with action aaa and one from ρ1\rho_1ρ1​ to ρ2\rho_2ρ2​ with action bbb, allocating time fractions τ\tauτ and 1−τ1-\tau1−τ. By qqq-homogeneity, the concatenated action is τ1−qa+(1−τ)1−qb\tau^{1-q}a+(1-\tau)^{1-q}bτ1−qa+(1−τ)1−qb. Optimizing over τ\tauτ gives (a1/q+b1/q)q(a^{1/q}+b^{1/q})^q(a1/q+b1/q)q, hence the triangle inequality after taking the qqq-th root and letting the two actions approach their infima.

Without homogeneity or nondegeneracy, AA\mathcal A_AAA​ remains a useful action principle, but its root need not define a distance.

Example: Wasserstein-p Action

The usual Wp\Wass_pWp​ distances correspond to changing only the homogeneity in the momentum. The case p=2p=2p=2 is the original Benamou--Brenier formula Benamou & Brenier, 2000; for 1<p<+∞1<p<+\infty1<p<+∞, the same dynamic viewpoint gives the standard description of absolutely continuous curves in Wasserstein spaces Ambrosio et al., 2006Villani, 2003Santambrogio, 2015:

Wpp(α0,α1)=inf⁡∂tαt+∇⋅(αtvt)=0αt=0=α0, αt=1=α1∫01 ⁣∫Rd∣vt(x)∣p  dαt(x)  dt.\Wass_p^p(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) = \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\alpha_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\alpha_t v_t)=0\\ \alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0,\ \alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1}} \int_0^1\!\int_{\RR^d} |v_t(x)|^p\,\d\alpha_t(x)\,\d t.Wpp​(α0​,α1​)=∂t​αt​+∇⋅(αt​vt​)=0αt=0​=α0​, αt=1​=α1​​inf​∫01​∫Rd​∣vt​(x)∣pdαt​(x)dt.
(45)

When αt=ρt  dx\alpha_t=\rho_t\,\d xαt​=ρt​dx and mt=ρtvtm_t=\rho_t v_tmt​=ρt​vt​, this is equivalently written with the convex perspective action

Ap(ρ,m)={∣m∣p/ρp−1,ρ>0,0,(ρ,m)=(0,0),+∞,ρ=0, m≠0.A_p(\rho,m)= \begin{cases} |m|^p/\rho^{p-1}, & \rho>0,\\ 0, & (\rho,m)=(0,0),\\ +\infty, & \rho=0,\ m\neq 0. \end{cases}Ap​(ρ,m)=⎩⎨⎧​∣m∣p/ρp−1,0,+∞,​ρ>0,(ρ,m)=(0,0),ρ=0, m=0.​
(46)

This is precisely Proposition: Homogeneous Dynamic Actions Define Distances with q=pq=pq=p: the ppp-th root of the value is Wp\Wass_pWp​. The endpoint p=1p=1p=1 can be treated separately: the perspective becomes A1(ρ,m)=∣m∣A_1(\rho,m)=|m|A1​(ρ,m)=∣m∣, and the dynamic problem collapses to Beckmann’s formulation of W1\Wass_1W1​ Beckmann, 1952. In the local notation above, ℓAp,α(v)=∫∣v∣p dα\ell_{A_p,\alpha}(v)=\int |v|^p\d\alphaℓAp​,α​(v)=∫∣v∣pdα, while the squared tangent cost associated with the distance Wp\Wass_pWp​ is qp,α(v)=ℓAp,α(v)2/pq_{p,\alpha}(v)=\ell_{A_p,\alpha}(v)^{2/p}qp,α​(v)=ℓAp​,α​(v)2/p.

Example: Concave-mobility action

One can instead keep the quadratic dependence in mmm and change the mobility multiplying the velocity field. Dolbeault, Nazaret and Savare introduced this construction as a class of generalized transport distances adapted to nonlinear diffusion Dolbeault et al., 2009. For a concave function θ:I→[0,+∞)\theta:I\to[0,+\infty)θ:I→[0,+∞), set

Aθ(ρ,m)=∣m∣2θ(ρ),A_\theta(\rho,m)=\frac{|m|^2}{\theta(\rho)},Aθ​(ρ,m)=θ(ρ)∣m∣2​,
(47)

with the convention Aθ(ρ,0)=0A_\theta(\rho,0)=0Aθ​(ρ,0)=0 when θ(ρ)=0\theta(\rho)=0θ(ρ)=0, and Aθ(ρ,m)=+∞A_\theta(\rho,m)=+\inftyAθ​(ρ,m)=+∞ when θ(ρ)=0\theta(\rho)=0θ(ρ)=0 and m≠0m\neq0m=0. Since (s,m)↦∣m∣2/s(s,m)\mapsto |m|^2/s(s,m)↦∣m∣2/s is convex and decreasing in s>0s>0s>0, the concavity of θ\thetaθ makes AθA_\thetaAθ​ convex in (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m). The associated value

Wθ2(ρ0 dx,ρ1 dx):=AAθ(ρ0,ρ1)\mathsf W_\theta^2(\rho_0\d x,\rho_1\d x) \eqdef \mathcal A_{A_\theta}(\rho_0,\rho_1)Wθ2​(ρ0​dx,ρ1​dx):=AAθ​​(ρ0​,ρ1​)
(48)

is the quadratic case q=2q=2q=2 of Proposition Proposition: Homogeneous Dynamic Actions Define Distances, hence Wθ\mathsf W_\thetaWθ​ is an extended distance under the same nondegeneracy assumptions. The choice θ(ρ)=ρ\theta(\rho)=\rhoθ(ρ)=ρ recovers W2\Wass_2W2​. Other choices encode different geometry: θ(ρ)=ργ\theta(\rho)=\rho^\gammaθ(ρ)=ργ with 0<γ≤10<\gamma\leq10<γ≤1 changes the cost of moving dilute mass, while θ(ρ)=ρ(1−ρ/M)\theta(\rho)=\rho(1-\rho/M)θ(ρ)=ρ(1−ρ/M) on [0,M][0,M][0,M] models a volume-filling or exclusion effect, since mobility vanishes both at vacuum and at the maximal density. Under the usual positivity and lower-semicontinuity assumptions, Wθ\mathsf W_\thetaWθ​ becomes a genuine metric on each finite-distance component. It is comparable with W2\Wass_2W2​ on classes where θ(ρ)\theta(\rho)θ(ρ) is bounded above and below by positive multiples of ρ\rhoρ; otherwise zero-mobility barriers can make some pairs infinitely far apart. The corresponding nonlinear diffusion and gradient-flow PDEs are discussed in Section Generalized Dynamic Wasserstein Flows. The induced squared tangent cost is

qθ,α(v)=ℓAθ,α(v)=∫ρ(x)θ(ρ(x))∥v(x)∥2  dα(x),q_{\theta,\alpha}(v) = \ell_{A_\theta,\alpha}(v) = \int\frac{\rho(x)}{\theta(\rho(x))}\norm{v(x)}^2\,\d\alpha(x),qθ,α​(v)=ℓAθ​,α​(v)=∫θ(ρ(x))ρ(x)​∥v(x)∥2dα(x),
(49)

for α=ρ dx\alpha=\rho\d xα=ρdx. Hence this is a local Riemannian case whenever the multiplier ρ/θ(ρ)\rho/\theta(\rho)ρ/θ(ρ) is finite and positive.

Dynamic Unbalanced OT¶

Unbalanced dynamic transport is obtained by allowing mass to be created and destroyed along the path. The continuity equation is replaced by a balance equation, and the action penalizes both spatial motion and growth. This dynamic formulation underlies the Hellinger--Kantorovich and Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao metrics Liero et al., 2016Chizat et al., 2018; its equivalence with static entropy-transport and cone formulations is developed in Liero et al., 2018Chizat et al., 2018.

A representative quadratic action is

∂tρt+∇ ⁣⋅mt=st,∫01 ⁣∫(∣mt∣2ρt+κ2st2ρt) dx  dt,\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot m_t=s_t, \qquad \int_0^1\!\int \left(\frac{|m_t|^2}{\rho_t}+\kappa^2\frac{s_t^2}{\rho_t}\right)\d x\,\d t,∂t​ρt​+∇⋅mt​=st​,∫01​∫(ρt​∣mt​∣2​+κ2ρt​st2​​)dxdt,
(50)

with the same perspective convention as above. Equivalently, writing mt=ρtvtm_t=\rho_t v_tmt​=ρt​vt​ and st=ρtgts_t=\rho_t g_tst​=ρt​gt​, one minimizes ∫01∫(∣vt∣2+κ2gt2) dρt dt\int_0^1\int(|v_t|^2+\kappa^2 g_t^2)\d\rho_t\d t∫01​∫(∣vt​∣2+κ2gt2​)dρt​dt under ∂tρt+∇ ⁣⋅(ρtvt)=gtρt\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\!\cdot(\rho_t v_t)=g_t\rho_t∂t​ρt​+∇⋅(ρt​vt​)=gt​ρt​. The parameter κ\kappaκ fixes the relative cost of reaction and transport.

Proposition: Static/Dynamic Equivalence for Unbalanced OT

Fix the action above and let CWκ\mathcal C\mathcal W_\kappaCWκ​ be the cone value with the cone metric normalized to the same growth scale κ\kappaκ. For nonnegative finite measures α0,α1\alpha_0,\alpha_1α0​,α1​ on Rd\RR^dRd, the dynamic value

WFR⁡κ2(α0,α1):=inf⁡∂tρt+∇⋅mt=stρ0=α0, ρ1=α1∫01Aκ(ρt,mt,st)  dt\WFR_\kappa^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) \eqdef \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\rho_t+\nabla\cdot m_t=s_t\\ \rho_0=\alpha_0,\ \rho_1=\alpha_1}} \int_0^1 \mathcal A_\kappa(\rho_t,m_t,s_t)\,\d tWFRκ2​(α0​,α1​):=∂t​ρt​+∇⋅mt​=st​ρ0​=α0​, ρ1​=α1​​inf​∫01​Aκ​(ρt​,mt​,st​)dt
(51)

equals the static cone formulation CWκ(α0,α1)\mathcal C\mathcal W_\kappa(\alpha_0,\alpha_1)CWκ​(α0​,α1​). Hence the static unbalanced problem and the balance-equation least-action problem define the same geodesic distance.

Proof

The cone construction turns variation of mass into radial motion and spatial transport into angular motion on C[Rd]\mathfrak C[\RR^d]C[Rd]. Applying the Benamou--Brenier theorem on the cone to the lifted endpoint measures gives a dynamic least-action problem on C[Rd]\mathfrak C[\RR^d]C[Rd] whose static value is the cone value. Projecting a cone curve back to the base space with weight r2r^2r2 produces a measure curve, a spatial flux and a source term satisfying the balance equation. Conversely, any finite-action triple can be lifted to a cone curve with the same relaxed action. This gives the static/dynamic identity; see Liero et al., 2016Liero et al., 2018Chizat et al., 2018Chizat et al., 2018.

show_book_figure("dynamic-unbalanced-geodesic")

Balanced and unbalanced Sinkhorn-barycenter interpolations between two one-dimensional Gaussian mixtures with swapped modal masses. The balanced row conserves total mass, so excess mass from the dominant left mode must move along the line toward the dominant right target mode, producing transient mass in the middle. The unbalanced row uses KL-relaxed marginal constraints; mass can be attenuated near overrepresented modes and recreated near underrepresented modes, giving a reaction--transport interpolation closer to the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao intuition.

Dynamic Spectral Wasserstein Distances¶

The static spectral distances of Spectral and Robust Wasserstein Distances penalize a coupling through the covariance of its displacement. A dynamic version keeps the continuity equation but replaces the pointwise kinetic energy by a gauge of the whole velocity covariance. The resulting action is nonlocal in space: velocity directions are charged globally through their covariance, rather than independently at each point.

Let γ\gammaγ be a monotone spectral gauge on S+d\mathbb S_+^dS+d​. For a probability measure α\alphaα and a velocity field v∈L2(α;Rd)v\in L^2(\alpha;\RR^d)v∈L2(α;Rd), define

Nγ,α(v)2:=γ ⁣(∫v(x)v(x)⊤ dα(x)).\mathcal N_{\gamma,\alpha}(v)^2 \eqdef \gamma\!\left(\int v(x)v(x)^\top\d\alpha(x)\right).Nγ,α​(v)2:=γ(∫v(x)v(x)⊤dα(x)).
(52)

In the local-action notation of (34), this means qγ,α(v)=Nγ,α(v)2q_{\gamma,\alpha}(v)=\mathcal N_{\gamma,\alpha}(v)^2qγ,α​(v)=Nγ,α​(v)2. The trace gauge gives the usual Wasserstein tangent norm, while the operator gauge γ(M)=λmax⁡(M)\gamma(M)=\lambda_{\max}(M)γ(M)=λmax​(M) charges only the largest directional velocity variance. The associated dynamic action distance is

Wγ,dyn2(α0,α1):=inf⁡∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0αt=0=α0, αt=1=α1∫01Nγ,αt(vt)2  dt.\mathsf W_{\gamma,\mathrm{dyn}}^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) \eqdef \inf_{\substack{\partial_t\alpha_t+\diverg(\alpha_t v_t)=0\\ \alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0,\ \alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1}} \int_0^1 \mathcal N_{\gamma,\alpha_t}(v_t)^2\,\d t .Wγ,dyn2​(α0​,α1​):=∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0αt=0​=α0​, αt=1​=α1​​inf​∫01​Nγ,αt​​(vt​)2dt.
(53)

In density--momentum variables, the instantaneous action is

(ρ,m)⟼γ ⁣(∫m(x)m(x)⊤ρ(x)  dx).(\rho,m) \longmapsto \gamma\!\left(\int \frac{m(x)m(x)^\top}{\rho(x)}\,\d x\right).(ρ,m)⟼γ(∫ρ(x)m(x)m(x)⊤​dx).
(54)

This functional is convex in (ρ,m)(\rho,m)(ρ,m) by the matrix perspective, together with the monotonicity and convexity of γ\gammaγ. It is nevertheless not, in general, a pointwise action density of the form ∫A(ρ(x),m(x))  dx\int A(\rho(x),m(x))\,\d x∫A(ρ(x),m(x))dx, because the covariance is computed globally before applying γ\gammaγ. It becomes local only for linear spectral gauges. For instance, if γ(M)=tr⁡(GM)\gamma(M)=\operatorname{tr}(GM)γ(M)=tr(GM) with G⪰0G\succeq0G⪰0, then the spectral action is the integral of the quadratic density

Alin(ρ,m)=m⊤Gmρ,A_{\mathrm{lin}}(\rho,m)=\frac{m^\top G m}{\rho},Alin​(ρ,m)=ρm⊤Gm​,
(55)

and the trace gauge, G=IdG=\IdG=Id in γ(M)=tr⁡(GM)\gamma(M)=\operatorname{tr}(GM)γ(M)=tr(GM), recovers the usual Benamou--Brenier action.

The following result, in the form used for normalized spectral flows in Peyré, 2026, shows that this dynamic construction is not merely infinitesimal: it exactly recovers the static displacement-covariance formulation.

Nonlocal Wasserstein Distances¶

The continuum dynamic distances introduced above are local: mass moves continuously through a velocity field and a continuity equation. For jump processes and heavy-tailed dynamics, the relevant motion is instead nonlocal: mass can jump directly from xxx to yyy. Erbar’s construction Erbar, 2012, building on generalized transport metrics with nonlinear mobilities Dolbeault et al., 2009 and connected to the discrete Markov-chain geometries of Maas and Mielke Maas, 2011Mielke, 2013, replaces the local gradient by a pairwise difference over (x,y)(x,y)(x,y).

The mechanism is the same as in the finite-state Markov-chain construction recalled at the end of this section. A graph edge i∼ji\sim ji∼j is replaced by a pair (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) sampled from a symmetric jump measure, finite sums over edges become integrals over X×XX\times XX×X, and the discrete difference ψi−ψj\psi_i-\psi_jψi​−ψj​ becomes a nonlocal increment. The same logarithmic mean θ\thetaθ appears in both settings because θ(a,b)(log⁡a−log⁡b)=a−b\theta(a,b)(\log a-\log b)=a-bθ(a,b)(loga−logb)=a−b is the algebraic chain rule that makes the entropy gradient flow coincide with the underlying reversible Markov or jump evolution.

This construction therefore does not fit the pointwise local action-density formalism A(ρ(x),m(x))A(\rho(x),m(x))A(ρ(x),m(x)) used above. Its action is still quadratic, but the tangent variable is an antisymmetric jump velocity v(x,y)v(x,y)v(x,y), and the mobility depends simultaneously on the two endpoint densities ρ(x)\rho(x)ρ(x) and ρ(y)\rho(y)ρ(y). It is best viewed as a convex action on the pair space X×XX\times XX×X, rather than as an integral of independent costs attached to single base points xxx.

Let (X,m)(X,\mathfrak m)(X,m) be a reference measure space, and let K(x, dy)K(x,\d y)K(x,dy) be a nonnegative jump kernel, reversible with respect to m\mathfrak mm. This means that J( dx, dy)=K(x, dy)m( dx)\mathsf J(\d x,\d y)=K(x,\d y)\mathfrak m(\d x)J(dx,dy)=K(x,dy)m(dx) is symmetric on X×XX\times XX×X. For a density ρ= dα/ dm\rho=\d\alpha/\d\mathfrak mρ=dα/dm, write

(60)

with θ(a,a)=a\theta(a,a)=aθ(a,a)=a. A curve αt=ρtm\alpha_t=\rho_t\mathfrak mαt​=ρt​m driven by an antisymmetric velocity vt(x,y)=−vt(y,x)v_t(x,y)=-v_t(y,x)vt​(x,y)=−vt​(y,x) satisfies the nonlocal continuity equation if, for all test functions φ\varphiφ,

 d dt∫φ  dαt=12∬∇ˉφ(x,y) vt(x,y) θ(ρt(x),ρt(y)) J( dx, dy).\frac{\d}{\d t}\int \varphi\,\d\alpha_t = \frac12 \iint \bar\nabla\varphi(x,y)\, v_t(x,y)\, \theta(\rho_t(x),\rho_t(y))\, \mathsf J(\d x,\d y).dtd​∫φdαt​=21​∬∇ˉφ(x,y)vt​(x,y)θ(ρt​(x),ρt​(y))J(dx,dy).
(61)

AK(ρ,v):=12∬∣v(x,y)∣2θ(ρ(x),ρ(y)) J( dx, dy),\mathcal A_K(\rho,v) \eqdef \frac12 \iint |v(x,y)|^2 \theta(\rho(x),\rho(y))\, \mathsf J(\d x,\d y),AK​(ρ,v):=21​∬∣v(x,y)∣2θ(ρ(x),ρ(y))J(dx,dy),

Under the regularity and irreducibility assumptions of Erbar (2012), WK\mathcal W_KWK​ is an extended distance on the set of probability measures absolutely continuous with respect to m\mathfrak mm, and finite-distance pairs are connected by constant-speed geodesics.

We use the analytic compactness and lower-semicontinuity theorem of Erbar (2012) for the logarithmic-mean action. Namely, action-bounded sequences of admissible curves are compact for the narrow topology, the weak nonlocal continuity equation is closed under this convergence, and the action is lower semicontinuous.

Kernelized Benamou--Brenier Distances¶

A different way to deform the Benamou--Brenier geometry is to keep the local continuity equation but to measure velocities in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space rather than in L2(α)L^2(\alpha)L2(α). This construction is motivated by Stein variational gradient descent, studied later in Stein Variational Gradient Descent: the kernel makes the velocity field smooth and computable from particles, at the price of defining a much more restrictive transport geometry.

Let kkk be a positive definite kernel on Rd\RR^dRd with scalar RKHS Hk\RKHS_kHk​. The vector-valued RKHS is

Hkd:=Hk×⋯×Hk,∥v∥Hkd2:=∑ℓ=1d∥vℓ∥Hk2.\RKHS_k^d\eqdef \RKHS_k\times\cdots\times\RKHS_k, \qquad \norm{v}_{\RKHS_k^d}^2 \eqdef \sum_{\ell=1}^d\norm{v_\ell}_{\RKHS_k}^2.Hkd​:=Hk​×⋯×Hk​,∥v∥Hkd​2​:=ℓ=1∑d​∥vℓ​∥Hk​2​.
(68)

This is the vector-valued analogue of the scalar RKHS norm used for MMDs in Dual RKHS Norms and Maximum Mean Discrepancies. The kernelized dynamic action between two probabilities is defined by

Wk2(α0,α1):=inf⁡αt,vt∫01∥vt∥Hkd2  dt,∂tαt+div⁡(αtvt)=0,\mathcal W_k^2(\alpha_0,\alpha_1) \eqdef \inf_{\alpha_t,v_t} \int_0^1\norm{v_t}_{\RKHS_k^d}^2\,\d t, \qquad \partial_t\alpha_t+\operatorname{div}(\alpha_t v_t)=0,Wk2​(α0​,α1​):=αt​,vt​inf​∫01​∥vt​∥Hkd​2​dt,∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0,
(69)

with endpoint constraints αt=0=α0\alpha_{t=0}=\alpha_0αt=0​=α0​ and αt=1=α1\alpha_{t=1}=\alpha_1αt=1​=α1​. This type of Stein geometry was introduced in the analysis of SVGD by Liu and Wang Liu & Wang, 2016Liu, 2017 and later developed geometrically in Duncan et al., 2019Nüsken & Renger, 2021. The corresponding tangent action is qk,α(v)=∥v∥Hkd2q_{k,\alpha}(v)=\norm{v}_{\RKHS_k^d}^2qk,α​(v)=∥v∥Hkd​2​, with the important caveat that the admissible tangent space is the smooth RKHS class, not the whole Wasserstein tangent space.

One should read the square root of (69) as an extended distance on finite-action components, not as a replacement for W2\Wass_2W2​ on all of P2(Rd)\Pp_2(\RR^d)P2​(Rd). If kkk is smooth enough that Hkd\RKHS_k^dHkd​ embeds into Lipschitz vector fields, finite-action curves are induced by regular flows. Atomic measures remain atomic with the same number of atoms, so a Dirac mass cannot be transported at finite kernelized action to a measure with a density. This lack of splitting is precisely what makes the geometry useful for deterministic particle methods, and also what makes it a nontrivial extended object rather than a full probability metric.

Discrete Wasserstein Distances on Markov Chains¶

The Benamou--Brenier construction also has a finite-state analogue, but not the naive one obtained by putting the Euclidean metric on the simplex. The key idea, introduced by Maas and independently developed in related forms by Mielke and by Chow--Huang--Li--Zhou, is to use the transition graph of a reversible Markov chain to define the admissible directions and the mobility of the mass Maas, 2011Mielke, 2013Chow et al., 2012. The entropy gradient-flow interpretation is stated later in Proposition: Entropy Gradient Flow of a Reversible Markov Chain.

Let X={1,…,n}\mathcal X=\{1,\ldots,n\}X={1,…,n} and let K=(Kij)K=(K_{ij})K=(Kij​) denote the off-diagonal transition rates of an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain reversible with respect to a probability vector π\piπ, so that πiKij=πjKji\pi_iK_{ij}=\pi_jK_{ji}πi​Kij​=πj​Kji​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j. Write a probability p∈Σnp\in\Sigma_np∈Σn​ in density form pi=πiρip_i=\pi_i\rho_ipi​=πi​ρi​, where

Σn:={p∈R+n:∑ipi=1}.\Sigma_n\eqdef\left\{p\in\RR_+^n:\sum_i p_i=1\right\}.Σn​:={p∈R+n​:i∑​pi​=1}.
(70)

The entropy relative to π\piπ is

Ent⁡π(ρ):=∑iπiρilog⁡ρi.\operatorname{Ent}_\pi(\rho)\eqdef\sum_i\pi_i\rho_i\log\rho_i.Entπ​(ρ):=i∑​πi​ρi​logρi​.
(71)

The logarithmic mean

θ(a,b):={a−blog⁡a−log⁡b,a≠b,a,a=b,\theta(a,b)\eqdef \begin{cases} \displaystyle\frac{a-b}{\log a-\log b}, & a\neq b,\\[.4em] a, & a=b, \end{cases}θ(a,b):=⎩⎨⎧​loga−logba−b​,a,​a=b,a=b,​
(72)

is the mobility selected so that entropy gradient flows recover exactly the Markov evolution. The reason is the edge-wise chain rule θ(a,b)(log⁡a−log⁡b)=a−b\theta(a,b)(\log a-\log b)=a-bθ(a,b)(loga−logb)=a−b, which converts entropy gradients into density differences along graph edges. For a potential ψ∈Rn\psi\in\RR^nψ∈Rn, define

(Kρψ)i:=∑jKijθ(ρi,ρj)(ψi−ψj),(\mathcal K_\rho\psi)_i \eqdef \sum_j K_{ij}\theta(\rho_i,\rho_j)(\psi_i-\psi_j),(Kρ​ψ)i​:=j∑​Kij​θ(ρi​,ρj​)(ψi​−ψj​),
(73)

with action

A(ρ,ψ):=12∑i,jπiKijθ(ρi,ρj)(ψi−ψj)2.\mathcal A(\rho,\psi) \eqdef \frac12\sum_{i,j}\pi_iK_{ij}\theta(\rho_i,\rho_j)(\psi_i-\psi_j)^2.A(ρ,ψ):=21​i,j∑​πi​Kij​θ(ρi​,ρj​)(ψi​−ψj​)2.
(74)

This is the finite-state squared tangent action qK,ρ(ψ)q_{K,\rho}(\psi)qK,ρ​(ψ); the tangent variable is the potential ψ\psiψ, or equivalently the induced edge flux, rather than an ambient Euclidean vector field.

The discrete transport distance is

WK2(ρ0,ρ1):=inf⁡ρt,ψt∫01A(ρt,ψt)  dt,ρ˙t+Kρtψt=0,\mathcal W_K^2(\rho^0,\rho^1) \eqdef \inf_{\rho_t,\psi_t} \int_0^1\mathcal A(\rho_t,\psi_t)\,\d t, \qquad \dot\rho_t+\mathcal K_{\rho_t}\psi_t=0,WK2​(ρ0,ρ1):=ρt​,ψt​inf​∫01​A(ρt​,ψt​)dt,ρ˙​t​+Kρt​​ψt​=0,
(75)

with endpoints ρ0=ρ0\rho_0=\rho^0ρ0​=ρ0, ρ1=ρ1\rho_1=\rho^1ρ1​=ρ1. Equivalently, one can write the same formula in edge-flux variables: flux is only allowed along edges where Kij>0K_{ij}>0Kij​>0, and the denominator in the kinetic energy is the logarithmic mean of the two endpoint densities.

The first nontrivial finite Markov geometries already show how the logarithmic mean bends the simplex. In both examples below, take the uniform random walk on the complete neighbor graph, so πi=1/n\pi_i=1/nπi​=1/n and Kij=1/(n−1)K_{ij}=1/(n-1)Kij​=1/(n−1) for i≠ji\neq ji=j.

Example: Two-point complete graph

On Σ2\Sigma_2Σ2​, write p=(r,1−r)p=(r,1-r)p=(r,1−r) and q=(s,1−s)q=(s,1-s)q=(s,1−s). Since there is only one edge, the discrete dynamic problem reduces to the scalar Riemannian length

WK(p,q)=∣∫sr duθ(u,1−u)∣,0<r,s<1.\mathcal W_K(p,q) = \left|\int_s^r \frac{\d u}{\sqrt{\theta(u,1-u)}}\right|, \qquad 0<r,s<1.WK​(p,q)=∣∣​∫sr​θ(u,1−u)​du​∣∣​,0<r,s<1.
(76)

This formula is closed but not Euclidean: the logarithmic mean changes the cost of moving mass depending on the current split between the two points.

Example: Three-point complete graph

On Σ3\Sigma_3Σ3​, the complete-neighbor graph is a triangle. For p∈int⁡(Σ3)p\in\operatorname{int}(\Sigma_3)p∈int(Σ3​), set

aij(p):=12θ(pi,pj),1≤i<j≤3.a_{ij}(p)\eqdef\frac12\theta(p_i,p_j), \qquad 1\leq i<j\leq3.aij​(p):=21​θ(pi​,pj​),1≤i<j≤3.
(77)

For a tangent vector u∈R3u\in\RR^3u∈R3 with u1+u2+u3=0u_1+u_2+u_3=0u1​+u2​+u3​=0, orient the edges as 1→21\to21→2, 1→31\to31→3, 2→32\to32→3. The squared norm induced by the discrete Wasserstein metric is

∥u∥p2=min⁡q12,q13,q23{q122a12+q132a13+q232a23},\|u\|_p^2 = \min_{q_{12},q_{13},q_{23}} \left\{ \frac{q_{12}^2}{a_{12}}+ \frac{q_{13}^2}{a_{13}}+ \frac{q_{23}^2}{a_{23}} \right\},∥u∥p2​=q12​,q13​,q23​min​{a12​q122​​+a13​q132​​+a23​q232​​},
(78)

subject to

u1+q12+q13=0,u2−q12+q23=0,u3−q13−q23=0.u_1+q_{12}+q_{13}=0, \qquad u_2-q_{12}+q_{23}=0, \qquad u_3-q_{13}-q_{23}=0.u1​+q12​+q13​=0,u2​−q12​+q23​=0,u3​−q13​−q23​=0.
(79)

Eliminating the three edge fluxes gives an explicit formula. With D=a12−1+a13−1+a23−1D=a_{12}^{-1}+a_{13}^{-1}+a_{23}^{-1}D=a12−1​+a13−1​+a23−1​,

q12∗=u2/a23−u1/a13D,q13∗=−u1−q12∗,q23∗=q12∗−u2,q_{12}^*=\frac{u_2/a_{23}-u_1/a_{13}}{D}, \qquad q_{13}^*=-u_1-q_{12}^*, \qquad q_{23}^*=q_{12}^*-u_2,q12∗​=Du2​/a23​−u1​/a13​​,q13∗​=−u1​−q12∗​,q23∗​=q12∗​−u2​,
(80)

and ∥u∥p2\|u\|_p^2∥u∥p2​ is obtained by inserting these values in (78). Therefore

WK2(p0,p1)=inf⁡pt∈int⁡(Σ3)∫01∥p˙t∥pt2  dt,p0=p0,p1=p1.\mathcal W_K^2(p^0,p^1) = \inf_{p_t\in\operatorname{int}(\Sigma_3)} \int_0^1\|\dot p_t\|_{p_t}^2\,\d t, \qquad p_0=p^0, \quad p_1=p^1.WK2​(p0,p1)=pt​∈int(Σ3​)inf​∫01​∥p˙​t​∥pt​2​dt,p0​=p0,p1​=p1.
(81)

Thus the three-state distance is an explicit two-dimensional Riemannian geodesic problem on the open triangle. The formula is simple enough to compute directly, but it already shows the main difference with Euclidean geometry on the simplex: the local metric depends nonlinearly on the current density through logarithmic edge mobilities.
